notes:
I've written notes on all 28 verses below. My research tools ran out before I could check every verse, so some have thin coverage. Those gaps are listed at the end.

---

## Matthew 16: Research notes

### vv. 1–4: The demand for a sign

**v. 1**
- Enduring Word (David Guzik): the Pharisees and Sadducees were usually enemies, so their joining together shows how seriously they saw Jesus as a threat. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- Guzik also contrasts the two groups. The Pharisees believed in angels and the resurrection and longed for the Messiah. The Sadducees accepted only the written Hebrew Scriptures, worked with Rome, and were not looking for a Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- Guzik: Jesus had already done many signs. The leaders wanted a sign "from heaven," because tradition held that a sign done on earth might be a fake from Satan, while one from the sky was assumed to come from God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- Matthew Henry: every miracle Jesus did was already a sign. They wanted one of their own choosing, to satisfy curiosity rather than to meet anyone's need. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_016.cfm

**vv. 2–3**
- Guzik: they could forecast the weather from the sky but could not see the evidence that the Messiah had come. He quotes D.A. Carson: the fact that they ask for a sign proves they can't read the signs. Guzik also applies the verse to people today who ignore the signs of the second coming. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/

**v. 4**
- Guzik: signs by themselves convert no one. Believers can trust signs and wonders too much as a way to bring people to faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- Guzik: the "sign of Jonah" is Jesus' resurrection, as He explained in Matthew 12:39–41. He lists parallels: Jonah gave himself up so others could be saved, vanished from sight, came back after three days, and preached repentance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/

### vv. 5–12: The leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees

**vv. 5–6**
- Guzik: in Scripture, leaven is regularly a picture of sin and corruption. He quotes the Puritan John Trapp: false teaching works like leaven because it sours, swells, spreads and corrupts, all out of sight. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- Precept Austin: "watch out" and "beware" are Greek present-tense commands, meaning the disciples must stay alert all the time. This leaven can be subtle and can even look "spiritual." Both commands are in the present imperative calling for the disciples to continually be vigilant https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-16-commentary
- Precept Austin quotes J.C. Ryle: the warning was meant for the church in every age, not only for the disciples then. this saying of our Lord's about the "leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees" was intended for all time. It was not meant only for the generation to which it was spoken. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-16-commentary

**vv. 7–8**
- Matthew Henry: Jesus forgave the disciples for forgetting the bread. What He criticised was their "little faith." He wants His people to trust Him to provide even when their own carelessness got them into trouble. See how easily Christ forgave his disciples' carelessness, though it was in such a material point as taking bread; and do likewise. But that which he chides them for is their little faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_016.cfm

**vv. 9–10**
- Guzik: worrying about bread was strange, since they had just seen Jesus feed crowds of over 5,000 and 4,000. He names three faults: not understanding (ignorance), not trusting (unbelief), and forgetting what Jesus had already done. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/

**vv. 11–12**
- Matthew Henry: Jesus didn't spell out the meaning. He repeated the warning so the disciples had to work it out for themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_016.cfm
- Precept Austin: the leaven is false teaching, which is dangerous because it spreads. One older writer quoted there sees three kinds: Pharisee religion that is all outward show, Sadducee doubt about the supernatural, and Herodian worldliness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-16-commentary

### vv. 13–20: Peter's confession

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Caesarea Philippi was a mostly Gentile area full of shrines to Baal, a cave linked to the god Pan, and a temple to Caesar. Quoting William Barclay, he suggests Jesus chose to be compared against all the world's religions. Jesus asked the question to lead into the more important one that follows, not because He needed to know. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- Matthew Henry: ordinary people talked more freely with the disciples than with Jesus, so the disciples were the ones who knew what people were saying. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_016.cfm

**v. 14**
- Guzik: John the Baptist, Elijah and Jeremiah all stood up to corrupt rulers. People may have been hoping for a political deliverer. All these answers respected Jesus but fell short of who He really is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/

**v. 15**
- Guzik: each disciple had to answer for himself. Everyone who hears of Jesus faces this question, and our answer is what gets judged. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/

**v. 16**
- Guzik: Peter saw that Jesus was not only the Messiah but God Himself. Jews understood "the Son of the living God," used in a unique sense, as a claim to be divine. He quotes R.T. France: "living" may contrast the true God with the local gods worshipped there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- John Piper (Baptist): Jesus means He is the Messiah, and not merely a human one but the unique, divine Son of God. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/what-are-the-keys-of-the-kingdom-of-heaven

**v. 17**
- Guzik: God revealed this through Peter so naturally that Peter didn't realise it. He quotes Spurgeon: knowing about Jesus only by human reasoning brings no more blessing than the Pharisees got. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- LCMS Witness (Lutheran): when a Christian confesses Christ as Saviour, it is the Father at work through the gospel. https://witness.lcms.org/2022/the-promised-comfort-of-heaven/

**v. 18: Traditions really differ here.**
- **Commentators often list four main views:** the rock is (1) Peter, (2) the truth Peter confessed, (3) Peter's faith, or (4) Jesus. GotQuestions describes all four. https://www.gotquestions.org/upon-this-rock.html
- **Older commentaries (Bible Hub):** in Aramaic, which Jesus probably spoke, "Peter" and "rock" were the same word. Ellicott's note says people may fairly disagree on whether Peter is the rock. Another commentator on the page warns that denying any link to Peter goes against the language and is mostly driven by controversy. Whether he is to be identified with the rock of the next clause is, however, a question on which men may legitimately differ. https://biblehub.com/matthew/16-18.htm
- **Pentecostal / Calvary Chapel (Guzik):** the rock is best taken as Jesus, or as Peter's confession. Peter himself wrote that believers are "living stones" and Jesus is the cornerstone (1 Peter 2:4–5). Peter was the "first rock" among many. It is best to see them as referring to either Jesus Himself (perhaps Jesus gesturing to Himself as He said this), or as referring to Peter's confession of who Jesus is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- **Guzik on "church":** this is the first use of *ekklesia* ("church") in the Bible, long before Pentecost. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- **Baptist (Piper):** Jesus didn't say "on you." *Petra* means bedrock, not a loose stone. The bedrock is Jesus' teaching, with the truth of who He is at its centre. Peter stands for everyone who faithfully makes that confession. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/what-are-the-keys-of-the-kingdom-of-heaven
- **Reformed / TGC (Gregg Allison):** the rock is Peter, but because of his confession. Allison holds the two together and argues that separating Peter from his confession is a mistake. He rejects the Catholic papal reading. The rock is Peter by virtue of his confession. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/what-does-this-rock-refer-to-matthew-1618/
- **Reformers (Luther, Zwingli):** a bible.org study reports that both said the rock is Jesus. https://bible.org/book/export/html/6361
- **Roman Catholic:** Peter is the rock, and his successors as pope remain head of the Church. Catholic writers argue that *Petros* and *petra* are practically the same word, and that Matthew would have used *lithos* if he meant a small stone. Catholics argue that because Jesus makes Peter, the first pope, the rock of his Church, his papal successors, as Peter, remain head of the Christian Church on earth. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/peter-is-the-rock-upon-which-the-church-is-founded ; https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-rock-explains-the-papacy
- **Eastern Orthodox (OCA):** the rock is Peter's confession of faith, not Peter himself. Christ alone is the true foundation. In Matthew 16:18, the word "rock" refers to Peter's confession of faith, and not to Peter himself https://www.oca.org/questions/history/on-this-rock-i-will-build-my-church
- **Church Fathers:** Tertullian, Cyprian and Basil said the rock is Peter. Augustine said Christ. Chrysostom and Cyril of Jerusalem said the confession. https://bible.org/book/export/html/6361 . Chrysostom in his own words: the church is built "on the faith of his confession." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200154.htm
- **Modern scholarship (bible.org study):** the study concludes from the Greek wordplay that the rock is most likely Peter, but finds nothing in the verse about successors. It also reports that some scholars (Luz, Bultmann) doubt vv. 17–19 go back to Jesus, partly because "my church" seems too early. Cullmann thinks the words are genuine but out of their original order. https://bible.org/book/export/html/6361

**v. 19: The keys and binding/loosing (traditions differ)**
- **Background (Bible Hub commentaries):** the image comes from Isaiah 22:22, where Eliakim gets the key of David's house as the royal steward. Ellicott says the key made Peter a teacher, not a priest, and the same power went to all the disciples. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes it was extended to all the apostles in Matthew 18:18. The Pulpit Commentary sees Peter as "first among equals," first using the keys at Pentecost and with the Gentiles, with no successors in that special role. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/16-19.htm
- **Guzik:** rabbis "bound" or "loosed" by ruling how a point of the law applied. The apostles would set the boundaries for the new-covenant community. No Christian today has authority over another believer's conscience. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/what-should-we-bind-and-loose-on-earth-heaven-live-qa-september-7-2023-2/
- **Baptist (Piper):** the keys are Jesus' teaching, the "key of knowledge" (Luke 11:52). Any faithful Christian who proclaims it opens the kingdom to people. The Greek tense means "shall have been bound": our teaching matters, but God's will decides. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/what-are-the-keys-of-the-kingdom-of-heaven
- **Lutheran (LCMS):** the "Office of the Keys" is a spiritual power Christ gave to the church. It actually forgives the sins of the repentant and withholds forgiveness from the unrepentant, rather than just announcing it. The church hands its public use to called pastors. The same source describes the Catholic reading as papal supremacy. https://cyclopedia.lcms.org/display.asp?t1=k&word=KEYS.OFFICEOFTHE . A pastor's absolution is as valid as if Christ Himself spoke it (Small Catechism). https://witness.lcms.org/2022/the-promised-comfort-of-heaven/
- **Reformed (Monergism):** the keys mean deciding what is allowed in God's kingdom, forgiving and retaining sins in a *declaring* sense, and church discipline. https://www.monergism.com/doctrine-church?page=1
- **Roman Catholic (New Advent):** based on Isaiah 22, Christ meant to give Peter supreme authority over His Church. The Church Fathers often cite the verse as proof of the Church's power to forgive sins. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08631b.htm
- **Orthodox (OCA):** the keys were given to Peter after, and because of, his confession. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2025/06/29/101840-the-holy-glorious-and-all-praised-leaders-of-the-apostles-peter

### vv. 21–28: The cross and discipleship

**v. 21**
- Guzik: this shocked the disciples, who expected a conquering Messiah. Jesus' death was a "must" because of human sin and God's love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- Matthew Henry: when Jesus spoke of the cross, He spoke in the same breath of the joy ahead. Believers should look through their own suffering to the reward beyond it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_016.cfm

**v. 22**
- Guzik: Peter probably felt sure God had told him he was right. His problem was being too confident in his ability to hear God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/por/tew/matthew-16.html (the Portuguese edition of Enduring Word; the English summary says the same at https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/)

**v. 23**
- Guzik: a moment earlier Peter spoke for God; now he spoke for Satan. He didn't deliberately choose Satan. He let his mind settle on human things, and Satan used that. Guzik links this to the "leaven" of v. 6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- Henry Morris (quoted in Precept Austin): this was satanic persuasion, not possession. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-16-commentary
- Matthew Henry: Satan often tempts us through our closest friends, as with Adam through Eve and Job through his wife. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_016.cfm

**v. 24**
- Guzik: taking up the cross means real death to self, a one-way walk to execution, not giving things up now and then. Denying self means living for others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- Matthew Henry: self-denial is the first lesson in Christ's school. We should accept our cross as "our own." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_016.cfm
- Precept Austin: Jesus is not giving the terms of salvation here. Self-denial has never saved anyone from sin. Our Lord is not here giving the terms upon which God will give salvation, for self-denial never saved a soul from sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-16-commentary

**v. 25**
- Guzik: losing our lives with Jesus leads to resurrection life, the only way to really find life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-16/
- Precept Austin: living for others adds to life rather than taking from it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-16-commentary

**v. 26**
- Matthew Henry: the love of the world drowns people in ruin. Gaining the world at the cost of the soul is a terrible bargain. Nothing can be paid to buy back a lost soul (the Greek *antallagma*, "something given in exchange"). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_016.cfm

**v. 28**
- Guzik: Jesus said this to show that following Him is not only crosses and death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/por/tew/matthew-16.html
- Believer's Study Bible (quoted in Precept Austin): the verse is not about Christ's final return. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-16-commentary

---

**What I couldn't find:**

- Only a little on v. 28 (I couldn't look into the views that it refers to the Transfiguration, the resurrection or AD 70).
- Nothing from Wesleyan/Methodist sources (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com).
- No NET Bible notes and nothing from Bible Odyssey.
- Nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of vv. 24–26.

A next round could cover those, plus the Bible Hub commentary pages for vv. 18 and 28, and the rest of the Enduring Word page, which got cut off around v. 18.
